data.title: Columbia Financial, Inc. Announces CFO Transition
data.description:
Resignation of CFO Thomas Splaine, Jr.; Appointment of Dennis E. Gibney as Interim CFO
Company to Commence Search for Permanent Chief Financial Officer

FAIR LAWN, N.J., Nov. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Columbia Financial, Inc. (the “Company”) (NASDAQ: CLBK), the holding company for Columbia Bank (“Bank”), today announced that Thomas Splaine, Jr., Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of the Company and the Bank, has notified the Company and the Bank of his intent to resign from the Company and the Bank effective December 18, 2026 for personal reasons. Mr. Splaine’s resignation of employment did not result from any disagreement with the Company on any matter relating to the Company’s financial statements, operations, policies, or practices.

In connection with Mr. Splaine’s departure, Dennis E. Gibney, First Senior Executive Vice President and Chief Banking Officer of the Company and the Bank, has been appointed Interim Chief Financial Officer effective December 18, 2026. Mr. Gibney previously served as Chief Financial Officer of the Company and the Bank from 2014 through January 28, 2026. He will continue in his other positions at the Company and the Bank while he serves as Interim Chief Financial Officer.

The Company has engaged an executive search firm and commenced a search for a permanent Chief Financial Officer.

About Columbia Financial, Inc.

Columbia Financial, Inc. is a Maryland corporation organized as Columbia Bank's parent holding company. Columbia Bank is a federally chartered savings bank headquartered in Fair Lawn, New Jersey that operates more than 100 full-service banking offices and offers traditional financial services to consumers and businesses in its market area, including select counties in New Jersey, and Brooklyn and Staten Island New York.

data.title: Predictiv AI Announces Change to Board of Directors
data.description:
TORONTO, ON / ACCESS Newswire / November 27, 2026 / Predictiv AI Inc. (CSE:PAI)(FWB:7IT) (the "Company" or "Predictiv AI") announces the voluntary resignation of Rob Barlow, effective November 26, 2026.

As an independent director, Mr. Barlow played an important role in advancing the Company's transformation through its December 2025 reverse takeover transaction. His involvement included helping bring Suman Pushparajah and the technology businesses he principally owned, Shift Technologies Canada Inc. and HouseStack Holdings Inc., into Predictiv AI. The acquisition brought together the businesses, their technology assets and intellectual property under Predictiv AI, establishing the foundation for the Company's current focus on the development and commercialization of artificial intelligence solutions.

Having supported the Company through this significant period of transformation, and with other professional commitments requiring his attention, Mr. Barlow has decided to step down.

The Company thanks Mr. Barlow for his contributions and support in establishing the foundation for its next phase of development and wishes him well in his future endeavours.

The Company intends to appoint a new independent director to its Board of Directors in the near term.

About Predictiv AI Inc.

Predictiv AI Inc. is a Canadian artificial intelligence company developing vertical AI applications for defined industries. The Company's products address fleet operations and communications, including fleet management software, AI-based agents for voice, chat and SMS, and tools designed to support structured operational workflows. For more information, please visit www.predictiv.ai.

data.title: SMX Featured in The Denver Post Opinion Piece on the Future of Colorado's Recycling Economy
data.description:
NEW YORK CITY, NY / ACCESS Newswire / November 27, 2026 / SMX, a pioneer in molecular marking and digital material authentication technology, was featured this week in an opinion piece published by The Denver Post examining the need for greater transparency, traceability and accountability in Colorado's evolving recycling economy.

The article, titled "Colorado Has Built a Recycling Framework. Now It Needs Proof," was published on November 23 and addresses one of the most pressing challenges facing states as they implement ambitious environmental legislation: establishing credible proof that materials are being recycled and returned to the economy.

Colorado has made significant strides in advancing sustainability through its Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) legislation, which places greater accountability on manufacturers and producers for the lifecycle of packaging materials. The next opportunity lies in establishing the technological infrastructure to support those policies.

SMX's proprietary molecular marking technology and Digital Material Passport Platform (DMPP) are designed to address this challenge by giving physical materials a persistent identity linked to a secure digital record. The technology enables businesses to authenticate materials, establish chain of custody, document recycled content and create audit-ready records throughout the supply chain.

By making recycled materials identifiable and certifiable, SMX aims to help manufacturers, recyclers and regulators move beyond traditional reporting methods toward a system grounded in scientific proof.

The Denver Post placement comes as the national conversation around recycling increasingly shifts from environmental commitments to measurable outcomes, regulatory compliance and the economic competitiveness of recycled materials.

SMX's technology is designed to help bridge the gap between legislative ambition and industrial execution, providing the tools necessary to build a more transparent, accountable and commercially viable circular economy.

The Denver Post article is one in a series of recent media profiles about SMX. Other stories have run in Tech Crunch, Benzinga, Forbes, the Boston Herald, the Chicago Tribune, Los Angeles Tribune, Miami Herald, Time, and Rolling Stone, among others.

About SMX

SMX (Security Matters) PLC (NASDAQ:SMX)(NASDAQ:SMXWW) develops molecular marking, authentication and digital traceability technologies designed to bring transparency, accountability and trust to global supply chains. Through its proprietary technology and Digital Material Passport Platform, SMX enables materials to carry a persistent identity throughout their lifecycle, supporting regulatory compliance, supply chain integrity and the transition to a circular economy.

data.title: Foresight Receives Conditional Order of Approximately $1.3 million for Thermal 3D Perception Systems as Part of Indian Defense Autonomous Drones Project
data.description:
Initial order forms part of a previously announced commercial framework from January 2025 with a potential of up to $2.1 million; follows successful completion of end-customer validation, for autonomous drones’ application.

NESS ZIONA, Israel, Nov. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Foresight Autonomous Holdings Ltd. (Nasdaq and TASE: FRSX) (“Foresight” or the “Company”), an innovator in 3D perception systems and AI autonomous stacks, today announced that its wholly owned subsidiary, Foresight Intelligent Systems Ltd., has received a conditional and non-binding order from an Indian drone manufacturing company for thermal ScaleCam 3D perception systems. The order is valued at approximately $1.3 million and the systems are intended for integration into autonomous drones for the Indian defense forces.

The order is part of the commercial cooperation framework announced by the Company in January 2025 with a prominent Indian drone manufacturer that is a supplier of the Indian Ministry of Defense. That framework carried previously disclosed commercial potential of up to $2.1 million. The current order follows the successful completion of the validation of Foresight’s thermal ScaleCam 3D perception solution under the agreement.

The order is conditional and remains subject to certain conditions including the successful completion of trials with the Indian Navy, completion of the relevant procurement and commercial negotiation process, and receipt of all required governmental, export-control, and regulatory approvals, where applicable.

Foresight’s 3D perception solution, which uses stereoscopic long-wave infrared technology and integrates internal measurement unit sensors, is designed to maintain robust autonomous drone performances in challenging GPS-denied environments such as dense smoke, poor lighting and high temperatures, enabling the detection of fire source and all object detection while providing real-time information on the drone’s spatial positioning. These capabilities make the solution particularly well-suited for defense unmanned ariel vehicle applications.

“The receipt of this conditional order is an important step forward in our collaboration with our Indian partner and validates the successful completion of the development phase,” said Haim Siboni, Chief Executive Officer of Foresight Intelligent Systems Ltd. “We look forward to progressing through the remaining trials and procurement stages.”

About Foresight
Foresight Autonomous Holdings Ltd. (Nasdaq and TASE: FRSX) is a technology company developing advanced three-dimensional (3D) perception systems, AI autonomous stack, and cellular-based applications. Through its wholly owned subsidiaries, Foresight Intelligent Systems Ltd. (formerly known as Foresight Automotive Ltd.), Foresight Changzhou Automotive Ltd., and Eye-Net Mobile Ltd., Foresight develops both “in-line-of-sight” vision systems and “beyond-line-of-sight” accident-prevention solutions.

Foresight’s 3D perception systems include modules of automatic calibration and dense 3D point cloud that can be applied to different markets such as automotive, defense, autonomous driving, agriculture, heavy industrial equipment, and unmanned aerial vehicles.

Eye-Net Mobile develops next-generation vehicle-to-everything collision prevention solutions and smart automotive systems to enhance road safety and situational awareness for all road users in urban mobility environments. By leveraging cutting-edge artificial intelligence technology, advanced analytics, and existing cellular networks, Eye-Net’s innovative solution suite delivers real-time pre-collision alerts to all road users via smartphones and other smart devices within vehicles.

For more information about Foresight and its wholly owned subsidiary, Foresight Intelligent Systems, visit www.foresightauto.com, follow @ForesightAuto1 on X, or join Foresight Automotive on LinkedIn.

data.title: A 10% cap on credit-card interest rates? Holiday shoppers shouldn't bank on it.
data.description:
By Andrew KeshnerGenna Contino

An APR cap on credit cards is 'possible but not probable,' one analyst says

President Donald Trump said he would be willing to work with Democrats on an interest-rate cap for credit cards.

As Americans prepare to pull out their credit cards for the holiday shopping season, President Donald Trump is saying he's up for capping the interest rates they're paying on those cards.

An annual-percentage-rate cap would be one spot where he'd be open to dealing with an incoming wave of Democrats, Trump said Saturday. Earlier this year, Trump proposed a temporary 10% APR cap, but the idea didn't go far.

"I would do it," Trump told Fox News reporter Kayleigh McEnany, who asked the president if he would work with Democrats on rate caps. "I know some people would say it's not free enterprise, but what's free enterprise when you're sitting home and get a bill that some guy set up in an office on Park Avenue and they said, 'Let's charge a fee that's too high?' ... The interest is too high."

The idea of a rate cap is resurfacing as the costs of housing, food and gas put pressure on Americans' budgets. With some consumers raiding their emergency savings accounts or relying on credit cards more often just to afford essentials, affordability was one of the driving forces for voters during the midterm elections.

So are capped APRs really on the way? Don't bank on it.

A rate cap is "possible but not probable," Jaret Seiberg, an analyst and managing director at TD Cowen's Washington Research Group, said in a note. TD Cowen estimated that there's a 25% chance that Congress passes a rate-cap law before the 2028 election. Seiberg also noted that Trump was responding to a question from a TV reporter, not raising the issue himself.

"That distinction matters, as we would be more concerned if Trump was prioritizing the issue as it would suggest a White House push for action," Seiberg said in the note.

People on both sides of the issue say interest-rate caps boil down to affordability.

Lawmakers including Missouri Republican Sen. Josh Hawley, Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders and New York Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have expressed support for an interest-rate cap as a way for Americans to save money. After Trump's latest comments, Hawley said he's ready to pass a law on caps as well. Earlier this month, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, said she has a bill and she's "ready to go."

Credit-card holders are keen on the idea, with 77% saying they support the idea of an interest-rate cap, according to a 2024 LendingTree survey. Half of them said they should be capped at 10% or lower.

Banks, however, say it's a bad idea that will backfire. When the Fed raises the federal funds rate, credit-card APRs increase as well to account for higher borrowing costs. If those APRs were capped, banks say they would have to reduce access to credit for consumers and small businesses.

"When policymakers artificially restrict the interest rates issuers can charge to cover the risk of losses, lenders must respond by reducing the risk through tighter underwriting standards, reduced credit limits and other changes," the Consumer Bankers Association said in a statement.

Consumer advocates say a cap would be a win for shoppers who have been slammed by high prices and expensive borrowing costs.

During the third quarter, consumers were paying an average of 22.36% on their credit cards with a balance, according to Federal Reserve data. Americans owe $1.28 trillion in credit-card debt, according to New York Fed third-quarter statistics.

Prior to 2022, those rates had largely remained below 16%, according to Fed data.

Americans paid $160 billion in interest in 2024, according to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's most recent look at the consumer credit-card market. That was up from $105 billion in 2022.

Don't Short Yourself: The No. 1 mistake beginners make with travel cards, according to The Points Guy

"Banks' fearmongering about access to credit is a transparent effort to distract from the fact that credit-card interest rates are higher than they have ever been and far out of step with historical norms," said Mike Pierce, the executive director of Protect Borrowers, a nonprofit group that advocates for borrowers.

Protect Borrowers joined other groups that sent a letter in February to the U.S. Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs and the U.S. House Financial Services Committee supporting the advancement of a bill temporarily capping rates at 10%.

A 10% cap would save cardholders $100 billion, but would lead to a $27 billion reduction in rewards offered by credit-card companies for those with credit scores of 760 or lower, according to an analysis from the Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator. An 18% cap would save Americans $16 billion each year, and a 15% cap would save them $48 billion annually without impacting rewards, Vanderbilt said.

Matt Schulz, chief consumer-finance analyst at LendingTree, said banks' concerns about limiting credit access for consumers with imperfect credit are worth taking seriously, but pointed out that federal credit unions already cap interest rates at 18%. These credit unions are still able to offer rewards, but they're generally less lucrative than those offered by major banks.

"Credit-card rate caps aren't unheard-of in this country," Schulz said.

A 10% APR cap is unlikely to get past Congress's next round of legislation and a 36% cap would be too high for Democrats, said Ed Mills, Washington policy analyst at Raymond James. The Military Lending Act sets a 36% maximum rate on many credit products to servicemembers and their families.

"Where things get interesting is the rate cap for credit unions," or a compromise like that where there's a set rate and some wiggle room for regulators to move the rate higher, Mills said. Federal credit unions technically have a 15% APR cap, but its regulators have the ability to put the rate up to 18% - which is where it's been for years.

More clarity on the chance of rate caps will come in the first half of 2027, he said. That's after the holiday shopping season has come and gone.

A cap's probability "goes up the higher the rate is. It's unclear if there is a compromise that could happen," said Mills.

-Andrew Keshner -Genna Contino

data.title: Nvidia's stock has tumbled 27% over one chaotic month. The next big test lies in the week ahead
data.description:
An earlier version incorrectly stated when Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will speak to Congress. By Bill Peters

Jensen Huang faces tough questions from Congress this week. Good luck pinning him down, one analyst says.

This handout photo posted on Nvidia's official X account on Nov. 23 shows reinstated CEO Jensen Huang reacting to an ovation from employees upon his return to the company headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif.

After a month unlike any other for Nvidia, the chip maker at the heart of the artificial-intelligence boom and the stock market faces even more drama in the week ahead.

Newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang will face harsh questioning from U.S. lawmakers from both parties next week in Washington, D.C. During that stretch, Nvidia (NVDA) will also hold a large developer conference in the same city, which could shed light on new products.

In both events, Nvidia will try to repair its image and articulate its path forward, after Huang resigned earlier this month following reports that he had extramarital affairs, including with a woman believed to be a spy for China.

Nvidia's stock has dropped 27% in November through Wednesday, putting it on track for its worst monthly performance since it lost 32% in April 2022. That decline comes even after an 18.9% rally so far this week.

Huang's ouster, which lasted a little more than a week, initially lopped more than $1 trillion from Nvidia's market value. And it deepened concerns over national security, the lengths taken and possible exceptions made to restore Huang to his old job on Monday, and an economy and stock market seemingly dependent on one executive.

Huang is set to appear for closed-door transcribed interviews with three House committees on Tuesday. He will also appear before the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs on Thursday.

During those hearings, analysts say, lawmakers are almost certain to ask about Nvidia's relationship with China and the U.S. government, and what sensitive information Huang may have handed over to China, which looks for a leg up in the global AI race. There will also likely be questions about what Nvidia knew, if anything, about China's alleged access to its high-end chips - via smuggling, routing them through other nations or remote access - and the money behind it.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Jay Goldberg, an analyst at Seaport Research Partners who covers semiconductors, said that Huang appeared to have support among Nvidia's employees and shareholders. Attitudes in Congress - from Democrats worried about President Donald Trump and aggressive AI development to Republicans worried about economic threats from China - were more frigid.

"[T]he one thing that Democrats and Republicans can agree on is that the greatest entrepreneur of all time is somehow a target," he said. "Not to excuse what he's done, but everything's upside-down right now."

Still, Huang, if nothing else, knows how to work a room, Goldberg said.

"Having had the pleasure of trying to pin Jensen down on a live-mic Q&A session at an investor event in the past: Good luck to them," he said of lawmakers' efforts to press Huang for specifics. "He is incredibly charismatic and knows how to handle a microphone."

John Blank, chief equity strategist at Zacks Investment Research, also said Huang was the most personable of the tech titans. But he said Huang understood the gravity of the situation.

"To some degree, he is somewhat humbled from the last two weeks, and I expect him to take it seriously and be pretty straightforward here," Blank said. "I would be surprised if he was flip and super arrogant at this point in time."

Huang's return to the top post - with President Donald Trump's help - launched Nvidia's stock to its biggest one-day percentage gain in 23 years. But shares fell on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Blank said some investors may be short-covering during next week's hearings, as they recalibrate their bets based on any news. But he and other analysts said Nvidia's stock is unlikely to be affected by the hearing, at least in the short term.

"This is the opening salvo of at least a year of stuff, and the market's pricing in plenty of surprises for all of this," Blank said.

Huang and Nvidia still face investigations from Nvidia's board, Congress and regulators. Trump has said the U.S. government "has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to Nvidia poses any risk" to national security. But more scrutiny could come when Democrats take control of Congress next year.

Democratic Sen. Chuck Schumer, the Senate's current minority leader, has said Democrats would investigate "any wrongdoing" by Nvidia or the Trump administration, and look into discussions between the U.S. and China about Huang, and Trump's Nvidia stockholdings. The White House has said Trump's investment portfolio is managed independently, and that neither Trump nor his family "has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input" on the portfolio, according to multiple reports.

Schumer also called for stronger export controls. Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas has also criticized Nvidia's decision to bring Huang back to the company.

Other issues still hang over Nvidia's stock, such as the costs and financing of the AI buildout and Nvidia's role as a financier to other parts of the AI industry. Huang's remarks could affect the broader semiconductor industry if he reveals more details about the flow of chips into China, Blank said.

The hearings are likely to overshadow Nvidia's GTC conference, which runs from Monday through Thursday. Prior to this month's blowup at the company, Huang was set to deliver the keynote on Tuesday - the same day he appears before the House committees.

According to CNBC, Ian Buck, Nvidia's vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, was scheduled to speak in place of Huang. Were Huang to make an appearance, analysts said, it could give him a chance to rally the company. But there were also risks.

"It would be lost in the noise and the public spectacle of his return, so I don't know if it would be all that productive for him to be at GTC from a technical standpoint," said Cody Acree, an analyst at StoneX.

Acree said he would be watching for updates on the rollout of Nvidia's Rubin Ultra chips, seen as a key component of powering agentic AI. Otherwise, it would be an event for networking and discussions about things like copper connectivity.

"Up until very recently, semiconductors were so boring," Goldberg said. "There have been very few instances in which my CEOs ended up in front of Congress. So, brave new world."

-Bill Peters

data.title: Nvidia's stock has tumbled 27% over one chaotic month. The next big test lies in the week ahead
data.description:
By Bill Peters

Jensen Huang faces tough questions from Congress this week. Good luck pinning him down, an analyst says.

This handout photo posted on the official X account of Nvidia on Nov. 23 shows reinstated CEO of Nvidia Jensen Huang reacting to the ovation from employees upon his return to the company headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif.

After a month unlike any other for Nvidia, the chip maker at the heart of the artificial-intelligence boom and the stock market faces even more drama in the week ahead.

Newly-reinstated CEO Jensen Huang is set to face harsh questioning by U.S. lawmakers from both parties this week in Washington. During that stretch, Nvidia (NVDA) will also hold a large developer conference in the same city that could shed light on new products.

In both events, Nvidia will try to repair its image and articulate its path forward, after Huang resigned earlier this month following reports that he had extramarital affairs, including with a woman believed to be a spy for China.

Nvidia's stock has dropped 27% in November through Wednesday against that backdrop, which puts it on track for the worst monthly performance since it lost 32% in April 2022. That decline comes even after an 18.9% rally so far this week.

Huang's ouster, which lasted a little more than a week, initially lopped more than $1 trillion off Nvidia's market value. And it deepened concerns over national security, the lengths taken and possible exceptions made to restore Huang to his old job on Monday, and an economy and stock market seemingly dependent on one executive.

Huang is set to appear for closed-door transcribed interviews with three House committees on Tuesday. He will also appear before the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs on Thursday.

During those hearings, analysts say, lawmakers are almost certain to ask about Nvidia's relationship with China and the U.S. government, and what sensitive information Huang may have ultimately ended up handing over to China as that nation looks for a leg up in the global AI race. There will also likely be questions about what Nvidia knew, if anything, about China's alleged access to its high-end chips - via smuggling, routing them through other nations, or remote access - and the money behind it.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Jay Goldberg, an analyst at Seaport Research Partners who covers semiconductors, said that Huang appeared to have support among Nvidia's employees and shareholders. Attitudes in Congress - from Democrats worried about President Donald Trump and aggressive AI development to Republicans worried about economic threats from China - were more frigid.

"That that's the one thing that Democrats and Republicans can agree on, is that the greatest entrepreneur of all time is somehow a target," he said. "Not to excuse what he's done, but everything's upside-down right now."

Still, Huang, if nothing else, knows how to work a room, Goldberg said.

"Having had the pleasure of trying to pin Jensen down on a live-mic Q&A session at an investor event in the past: Good luck to them," he said of lawmakers' efforts to press Huang for specifics. "He is incredibly charismatic and knows how to handle a microphone."

John Blank, chief equity strategist at Zacks Investment Research, also said Huang was the most personable of the tech titans. But he said Huang understood the gravity of the situation.

"To some degree, he is somewhat humbled from the last two weeks, and I expect him to take it seriously and be pretty straightforward here," Blank said. "I would be surprised if he was flip and super arrogant at this point in time."

Huang's return to the top post - with President Donald Trump's help - launched Nvidia's stock to its biggest one-day percentage gain in 23 years. But shares fell on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Blank said that there may be some investor short-covering during next week's hearings, as investors recalibrate their bets based on any news. But he and other analysts say Nvidia's stock is unlikely to be affected by the hearing, at least in the short-term.

"This is the opening salvo of at least a year of stuff, and the market's pricing in plenty of surprises for all of this," Blank said.

Huang and Nvidia still face investigations from Nvidia's board, Congress and regulators. Trump has said the U.S. government "has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to Nvidia poses any risk" to national security. But more scrutiny could come as Democrats take control of Congress next year.

Democratic Sen. Chuck Schumer, the Senate's current minority leader, has said Democrats would investigate "any wrongdoing" by Nvidia or the Trump administration, and look into discussions between the U.S. and China about Huang, and Trump's Nvidia stock holdings. The White House has said Trump's investment portfolio is managed independently, and that neither Trump nor his family "has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input" on the portfolio, according to multiple reports.

Schumer also called for stronger export controls. Republican Senator John Cornyn of Texas has also criticized Nvidia's decision to bring Huang back to the company.

Other issues still hang over Nvidia's stock, such as the costs and the financing of the AI build-out and Nvidia's role as a financier to other parts of the AI industry. Huang's remarks could pose implications for the broader semiconductor industry, if he happens to reveal more details about the flow of chips into China, Blank said.

The hearings are likely to overshadow Nvidia's GTC conference, which runs from Monday through Thursday. Prior to this month's blowup at the company, Huang was set to deliver the keynote of that event on Tuesday - the same day he appears before the House committees.

According to CNBC, Ian Buck, Nvidia's vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, was scheduled to speak in place of Huang. Were Huang to make an appearance, analysts said, it could give him a chance to rally the company. But there were also risks.

"It would be lost in the noise and the public spectacle of his return, so I don't know if it would be all that productive for him to be at GTC from a technical standpoint," said Cody Acree, an analyst at StoneX.

Acree said he would be watching for any updates on the rollout of Nvidia's Rubin Ultra chips, seen as a key component of powering agentic AI. Otherwise, it would be an event for networking and discussions about things like copper connectivity.

"Up until very recently, semiconductors were so boring," Goldberg said. "There have been very few instances in which my CEOs ended up in front of Congress. So, brave new world."

-Bill Peters

data.title: Week Ahead for FX, Bonds: Key Labor Data in Focus -2-
data.description:
South Korea is scheduled to release its November trade and inflation data on Tuesday and Wednesday, with exports seen accelerating and consumer price growth easing.

Most analysts expect chip demand fueled by the artificial-intelligence boom to continue driving strong semiconductor exports, further widening the country's trade surplus.

For the first 20 days of November, the country's chip exports nearly quadrupled from a year earlier, keeping them on course for another monthly record.

Citigroup economist Jin-Wook Kim expects South Korea's exports to have climbed 105.4% from a year earlier, faster than revised 93.9% growth in October. He expects the country's trade surplus to widen to $53.6 billion from revised $42.6 billion in the previous month.

Inflation could moderate in November, Kim said in a recent note, as seasonally weaker price pressures from tourism services and agricultural products could outweigh inflationary pressures from pricier durable goods.

Citi expects the headline consumer price index to have risen 2.7% from a year earlier, slower than a 2.8% increase in October. On a monthly basis, the index is seen falling 0.27% after rising 0.25% in October, according to Citi estimates.

Indonesia

Indonesia's November inflation could ease moderately to 3.1% from 3.2% in October, as lower food prices offset some pressure from administered and core components, ANZ's economist Dhiraj Nim said.

Core inflation is expected to remain contained at around 2.6%-2.8%, suggesting price pressures are not yet broad-based. The reading should remain relatively benign for Bank Indonesia, though renewed food-price increases remain a risk, he added.

Resilient exports and a healthy non-oil and gas surplus continue to support Indonesia's trade balance, UOB economist Enrico Tanuwidjaja said. However, imports are growing faster than exports as domestic demand and investment pick up, pointing to a gradual narrowing of the trade surplus, he added.

Southeast Asia

Inflation will be the focus in Southeast Asia during the week, where prices likely eased in November.

The Philippines' headline consumer-price index should ease further in November, reflecting sharp declines in fuel prices, said ING economists. Headline CPI rose 7.8% in October, while core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 5.4%.

Core CPI likely remained relatively sticky due to still-firm services costs and underlying domestic demand, they added.

Thailand's headline inflation rate likely eased to 3.6% compared to a year ago in November from October's 3.9%, DBS economists said. The expected moderation in prices largely reflected easing energy price pressures, and softer food inflation, they added.

Hong Kong

Hong Kong will report October retail sales on Tuesday. Deutsche Bank Research expects Hong Kong's retail sales value and volume to grow by 5% and 3% year-on-year, respectively, in October, both moderating from September. "The stock market correction may have weighed on local consumer confidence," it says.

Hong Kong's economy has been strong this year. Semiconductor trade and Hong Kong's role in the broader global AI supply chain continued to underpin the city's economic growth, according to a research note by UOB.
